name: The Four Billion Year Old Story of Consciousness
description:
We tend to think of humans as special because of our superior intelligence, a story that runs from spotting poisonous berries to Descartes’ I think, therefore I am, and now, to the machines we worry will out-think us. This conversation asks a different question: was cognition ever really what made us human, or is that just the story intelligence tells about itself? 
The deeper question addressed is not how we came to think, but rather how we came to cooperate. In ancient times, capabilities were shared across a group: one read the stars, another tracked prey. Cognition was distributed, and cooperation was mutually beneficial. This discussion argues that perhaps, intelligence did not come first. Perhaps, consciousness evolved less to help us think, and more to help us stay together.

name: Directors' Cut
description:
Four directors, twenty years, and one building that didn’t always exist. 
Long before BIC had a building to call its own, it was but an idea. This conversation turns the lens on the institution itself, bringing together three directors to reflect on the different Bangalore International Centres they each inherited, built, and passed on. Structured as an AMA, the session draws questions from RSVPs, from BIC’s own staff, and from the audience in the room. 
From an institution without walls, to the construction and induction of its home, to the shaping of the team that runs it today, and now, into its next chapter — this open, unscripted conversation looks at what it takes to build and sustain an institution like this one, and what each director would like to see it become. 
This talk is part of a series marking twenty years of BIC. It is a chance to trace what has changed, what has endured, and how ideas evolve over time. BIC is proud to have been host to conversations that connect culture, ideas, and public life across two decades.

name: A Democratic View of Geopolitics
description:
In the map of the world we have long known, the US and Western powers stand at one pole, with Russia and China at the other: ideological, institutional, intentional. 
This discussion, based on the book The De-democratisation Project, argues that seismic shifts in the world, the genocide in Gaza, Russia’s war on Ukraine, the US-Israel war on Iran, cannot be understood through the outmoded West-versus-Rest lens. The true crisis of our time, it suggests, is a global attempt to undo the hard-won consensus that democracy and human rights are universal. The conversation imagines a different map altogether: one built on solidarity, and the shared aspiration of democracy.

name: The Many Pasts of Panipat, 1761
description:
A great “what if?” moment in Indian history, the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 has produced martyrs, ballads, and endless partisan debate. This lecture examines how its retelling, across school textbooks, Hindu nationalist historiography, and cinema, has flattened a complex event into a tale of heroes and villains. It raises the question, whose Panipat are we really remembering? 
The vernacular primary sources tell a different story: where popular memory insists on certainty, they equivocate, contradict, and complicate. A micro history of the battle reveals multiple pasts, remembered and recorded by multiple men. This lecture makes a case for why critical historians cannot ignore this plurality while narrating the event to a generation raised on a communal rendering of Indian history. 
About Satish Chandra 
Professor Satish Chandra (1922-2017) was one of India’s foremost historians and a towering authority on medieval Indian history. Over a distinguished four-decade career, he taught at leading universities across the country, including Allahabad University, Aligarh Muslim University, Delhi University, Rajasthan University, and finally Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). At JNU, he co-founded the Centre for Historical Studies alongside S. Gopal, Bipin Chandra, and Romila Thapar. As Chairman of the University Grants Commission, he went on to help shape academic life across India, and in 1985, deeply committed to intellectual exchange, he co-founded the Society for Indian Ocean Studies. A thoughtful historian who brought a Marxist approach to the field, Chandra’s work bridged eras and ideas, leaving an enduring mark on the study of India’s past.

name: Mystik Vibes
description:
Mystik Vibes is an Indo-Jazz musical journey by Amith Nadig, Muthu Kumar, and Aman Mahajan, a meeting point where the melodic language of Carnatic and Hindustani music finds kinship with the freedom of Jazz. Beneath three distinct traditions, the musicians uncover a single, shared pulse: improvisation, emotion, breath. If music can dissolve the boundaries between such different worlds, what else might dissolve, if we listened closely enough? 
Built almost entirely from original compositions, each piece carries the story of the musician who wrote it, and the friendship between all three. Every note becomes a small act of translation, one tradition speaking to another, until the differences soften and only the music remains. A short Q&A follows the performance, encouraging audiences to engage deeply with the experience.

name: From One Mind to Many
description:
Where does great science begin? 
This lecture explores how excellence in scientific research begins with the individual; with curiosity, rigour, and imagination, growing outward into the institutions and cultures that sustain it. 
Drawing on decades spent at the frontier of theoretical physics, Rajesh Gopakumar turns to a more urgent question: how can India nurture and nourish scientific excellence at every level, from the solitary researcher to the institutions built to support them? Great science, he argues, is never possible alone. 
This lecture is a part of Azim Premji University’s Public Lecture Series.

name: The Resurrection Quest
description:
121 min | English with subtitles | United States, China, Germany, Kenya, Russia, Singapore, UAE 
Blending science with emotional depth, this documentary is a cinematic essay on our relationship with life, death, and the illusions of control. Spanning seven countries, it explores humanity’s audacious pursuit of one of the most radical scientific frontiers of our time: the reversal of extinction. Is de-extinction hubris, or hope? 
From cloning pets and engineering extinct birds to reviving ancient ecosystems, the film offers an intimate, urgent look at the dream of second chances, and its consequences. At the heart of the films lies the concept of Samsara; a cyclical journey through grief, hope, death, and renewal. As species vanish and ecosystems unravel, the film follows scientists and conservationists chasing what was lost, be it a beloved dog, an extinct pigeon, the last northern white rhinos, or even a gene-edited, cold-resistant elephant standing in for the woolly mammoth. But beneath the technology lie harder questions still: who decides which species return, and who gets access to the tools that bring them back?

name: Songs of the Seeker
description:
This musical concert is inspired by the poetry and philosophy of the 15th-century mystic poet, Saint Kabir. Original compositions and reimagined bhajans carry Kabir’s timeless words into a new sonic world, where folk instruments and Indian melodic traditions meet electronic textures, vocal harmonies, and unexpected percussion. 
Everyday objects become instruments, and familiar sounds take on new forms, as the performance drifts between stillness and groove, meditation and momentum. Audiences are invited to listen, reflect, and sing along, becoming seekers themselves for an evening. 
The Sadho Project
The ensemble is a Bengaluru-based quintet reimagining Indian sound through electronic innovation, blending traditional motifs, field textures, and ambient layers. Their music unfolds where the pulse of machines meets the soul of melody, creating space for reflection and transformation.

name: India after Bhagat Singh
description:
Language: Hindi, Urdu, and English 
What happened to the fierce romanticism of Bhagat Singh’s revolutionary spirit? 
This solo play explores the profound changes the nation has undergone since the martyrdom of the legendary freedom fighter. Breathing new life into his revolutionary philosophy, the performance holds his core ideals of justice, equality, and freedom, up against modern-day socio-political scenarios. 
The soil of Jallianwala Bagh, the site of the massacre that revolutionised young Bhagat Singh, is not merely dirt preserved in an urn. It is a witness to systemic cruelty, unheeded cries, and human sacrifice. When destruction and violence unfold today, in Manipur, Kashmir, or the Hasdeo forests, the same soil bleeds again. The play asks: how many unrecognised Jallianwala Baghs must exist before humanity notices? Both a mirror to contemporary society and an urgent call to remember the true spirit of the nation’s struggle, this performance refuses to let history stay history.

name: Odyssey
description:
Odyssey explores the human experience through Bharatanatyam, weaving together compositions from various languages and composers, spanning centuries of tradition and feeling. From the carefree days of childhood to the wisdom of age, each of us walks a path shaped by emotion, experience, and meaning. What does it take to simply enjoy the ride? 
Revisiting the joy of childhood and the hope and love of youth, the piece reflects honestly on how expectations, ego, and anxiety can pull us from what truly matters. It also showcases the beautiful moments of the journey too: the moments we let go, open our hearts, and rediscover life’s deeper purpose.

name: Gandhi’s Long Shadow
description:
Gandhi’s ideas did not go unchallenged, even by those closest to his moment in history. This talk draws on the book Arguments with Gandhi, examining the ideological disagreements he had with Marxists, religious fundamentalists, economic modernizers, and anti-caste radicals. What can a century of disagreement teach us about how to live now? 
Using Gandhi’s legacy as a lens, the talk offers a moral and political history of the modern world, one built as much from argument as from agreement. Gandhi’s debates with his contemporaries, and later generations’ arguments with him, foreground questions we have yet to resolve: how do we resist political tyranny? How do we address discrimination based on caste, gender, and race? And how do we achieve freedom from poverty without destroying the planet along the way?

name: Shera
description:
20 min | Kumaoni with English subtitles 
All Monu can think about as he roams the forests with his best friend Raju, is spotting the elusive leopard, Shera, before his family moves away to the city. Time is running out, so Raju comes up with an idea: a little dangerous, but maybe just crazy enough to work. Will they find Shera in time? 
Watch the film, flip through the beautifully illustrated graphic book, and meet the storyteller behind it all! Shera began as a short film and grew into a graphic book, hand-painted by acclaimed artist Allen Shaw, bringing to life the magic and mystery of the Himalayan valleys of Kumaon. Beyond the adventure lies a story about home, moving away, and a community learning to share its world with a wild, wonderful neighbour. 

Around the World in 50 Sundays is a journey that begins, not with a ticket, but with opening a book. In a city like Bangalore where families are always in motion, the BIC Library hopes to offer stillness and a quiet, welcoming space for both parents and children where reading becomes a shared experience. Every Sunday, we open our doors to invite you into a library that listens; building a rhythm of return, a habit of joy and a new community bound not just by books, but by the weekly ritual of reading together.

We welcome your ideas and input. If you have suggestions for children’s events or activities that align with this vision, we’d love to hear from you. Please reach out to us at library@bangaloreinternationalcentre.org
